question: How does mucus help in passage of food?

supplied_evidence.text:
162 Coordination in life processesGovernment’s Gift for Students’ Progress
x Why do we salivate when you sleep during the day?
You have heard about Nocturnal animals, which are active during nights, but we
are active during daytime and take rest at night. All the systems of our body are active
in function during the time of our activity. Hence, man is a diurnal animal. Our
digestive system is also active in day time and ready to receive the food for digestion.
If we sleep during daytime saliva oozes out of our mouth and wets the pillows. This
will not happen during night time. We secrete 1-1.5 liters of saliva per day.

The walls of the food pipe secrete a slippery
substance called mucus. Mucus lubricates and
protects the oesophageal walls from damage. This
helps the food bolus to slide down easily just as
the oiled potatoes that move in the tube. Besides
this, the saliva in the bolus also aids in easy
movement of food, which moves into the stomach.Fig-6: Peristaltic movement of bolus in

The wall of the oesophagus is made up of two kinds of smooth muscles.
The inner layer consists of circular muscles and the outer layer of
longitudinal muscles. Contraction of the circular muscles results in
narrowing of the oesophagus just behind the bolus. So the food is squeezed
downwards.
Contraction of the longitudinal muscles infront of the bolus widen
the tube, this results in shortening of that particular part of the oesophagus.
Contraction and relaxation of these muscles bring in a wave like motion
that propels the food bolus into the stomach by the action called as
“peristalsis” (you have studied about this in the chapter on nutrition). This
is involuntary and under the control of autonomous nervous system.
x What makes the movement of the food bolus in the oesophagus easy?
Think why people are advised not to swallow food without chewing
properly or do not eat in hurry.

parsed_output.answer: Mucus helps in the passage of food by lubricating the walls of the oesophagus. This makes it easier for the food bolus to slide down the oesophagus without causing damage to the walls. The mucus acts like a slippery substance, similar to oil in the experiment with the cycle tube and potatoes, which allows the food to move smoothly through the oesophagus by wave-like movements called peristalsis.
